psych.headline: People defer to AI more than its signals warrant
points: AI influence goes unnoticed: readers spotted AI-polished LinkedIn posts only 49% of the time, and the edits did not change perceived trust.

Trust cues and warnings do little: in 489,283 real chatbot exchanges, attribution and hedging rarely pushed users toward checking answers, and bias disclaimers on a political chatbot reduced persuasion only in some tasks and not after a week (1,586 participants).

Deference shows up in action: once chat history set a pattern, 75.0% of 360 participants sent the AI-drafted letter, and across 1,955 effects human-AI teams trailed whichever of human or AI was better alone.

edu.headline: How AI is used in learning matters more than whether it is used
points: Structured use pays off: physics students who followed a set worked-solution-then-practice cycle with AI largely reported better understanding (90.9%), and synced visual cues on AI-narrated slides raised comprehension over static slides.

Feedback changes teachers more than learners: in a randomized trial with 1,030 tutors, automated discourse feedback raised good teaching moves and learner reasoning by 8–15%, but tutors still did about 91.5% of the talking.
Being pleasant is not the same as being helpful: student teams warmed to a supportive AI teammate but rated a challenging one more helpful across five weeks.

tech.headline: Coding and security agents are capable but brittle over long or adversarial work
points: Long-horizon building is still hard: on chains of 5–15 dependent coding steps the best of nine frontier models solved only 18.5% of tasks.
Safeguards have gaps: signing agent-to-agent requirements cut unsafe actions from 69.4% to 9.0%, but one adversarial line added before signing pushed violations up to 75%.

Cheaper tooling works for focused tasks: small open-weight models on one consumer GPU reproduced most easier CyberGym vulnerabilities, and risk-based test selection caught 49–64% of bug-introducing commits while heavily testing only 20% of commits.

ai.headline: Agent performance hinges on scaffolding and on how it is measured
points: Changing what surrounds the model pays off: optimizing the agent's environment cut Haiku 4.5's cost by 72.7% with a 14.34% higher pass rate, and runtime self-improvement in Exo cut model costs 12–53%.
Benchmarks themselves move scores: fixing issues in about 30% of Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks raised accuracy over 10 points and shifted ranks by up to three.

Results are uneven and risk is not just capability: only 22 of 33 ServerBench runs produced a working system, and a loss-of-control score tracked failures across 13 frontier models (r = 0.84) independently of raw capability.

fin.headline: Careful testing is shrinking claimed edges, from AI agents to trading signals
points: AI agents are not ready to do finance work alone: none of 150 FINCOSMOS sessions passed, even when the simulated client was satisfied.
Strict tests deflate AI trading signals: under an anti-look-ahead protocol, LLM news signals fell to a daily information coefficient of 0.020 (t = 1.7) on blinded 2026 data.

Volatility is forecastable in crypto at fine scales: learned intraday weighting improved forecasts in all 54 comparisons (7–9% on average), and crypto volatility responds to trends with a lag peaking near 20 minutes.

papers.title: When History Overrides Intent: Relational Schema Lock-In in Human-LLM Interaction
papers.authors: Wei Yang
papers.summary: Once a chat history set a pattern, people tended to go along with the AI's version of the task: 75.0% of 360 participants sent the AI-drafted suspension letter, including 11 who had said their real intent was to cancel.
findings: Three studies: an analysis of user reports, a controlled test reproducing the history-driven behavior across six models, and a 360-person experiment.
75.0% of participants sent the AI's suspension letter; 11 of them had stated a final intent to cancel instead.
Pushing back openly against the AI lowered task completion, but the letters people did send stayed faithful to what they wanted.
papers.takeaway: Conversation history can quietly steer users away from their own goals, a risk for assistants with memory; the core experiment uses a single letter-writing scenario.
papers.evidence: Mixed methods · controlled experiment with 360 participants + 6-model test

papers.title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
papers.authors: Michelle Vaccaro, Abdullah Almaatouq, Thomas W. Malone
papers.summary: Pooling 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers, human-AI teams beat humans working alone but on average did significantly worse than whichever of the human or the AI was better on its own.
findings: Synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes drawn from 420 studies of human-AI collaboration.
Teams outperformed humans alone on average.
Teams fell significantly short of the best single performer (human or AI alone); the abstract gives no pooled effect size.
papers.takeaway: Adding a human to an AI (or vice versa) does not reliably create synergy, so team designs need testing; the pipeline is automated, so coding errors in extracted effects are possible.

papers.title: Out of sync: Accommodation, evaluation, and emergence in five weeks with an agentic AI teammate
papers.authors: Nia Nixon, Jaeyoon Choi, Pedro Martins de Bastos
papers.summary: Student teams warmed socially to a supportive AI teammate from the first session, yet rated it less helpful than a challenging AI teammate across all five weeks.
findings: 17 student teams (N = 48) in an undergraduate learning-analytics course worked with a persistent LLM teammate for five weeks.
The AI was given either a challenging (Cognitive) or an inclusive (Supportive) role; students used more social language with the Supportive one from session one.
Perceived collaboration and positive-affect words crossed over slowly over time; the abstract reports no effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: How students feel about an AI teammate and how useful they find it can move in opposite directions; it is one course with 48 students.

papers.title: Look Over There! Dynamic Visual Guidance for AI-Narrated Slides
papers.authors: Jiongning Allen Lian, Yutong Alison Mei, Ho Ting Cheung
papers.summary: Adding zooms and highlights synced to AI narration raised immediate comprehension and lowered perceived cognitive load compared with the same narration over static slides.
findings: Within-subjects study with 24 participants comparing GuideSlide to static slides with identical narration.
Dynamic guidance gave higher immediate comprehension scores and lower perceived cognitive load.
Participants strongly preferred the dynamic version; the abstract gives no numeric effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Cheap visual cueing could make AI-generated lecture videos easier to follow; 24 people and only immediate recall were tested.

papers.title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs
papers.authors: Raffaele Giancotti, Francesca Santucci, Amama Anjum
papers.summary: Most U.S. health-AI degree programs teach ethics (80.6%), but only 22.2% cover where training data comes from, and none of the seven master's programs met the study's main standard.
findings: 36 programs at 21 universities reviewed; ethics in 29 (80.6%), data provenance in 8 (22.2%), structural provenance in 6 (16.7%).
Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational fields and 3.3% from social sciences or humanities.
Among 51 instructors with known gender, 66.7% were men.
papers.takeaway: Future health-AI builders may learn ethics in the abstract without learning to question their data; this is a review of published curricula, not of what is taught in class.

papers.title: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families
papers.authors: Emmanuela Andam, Emanuel S. Grant, Naima Kaabouch
papers.summary: Modeling what malware does after infection as a graph of behaviors identified malicious samples with 94.44% accuracy, 7.4 MCC points better than a flat-feature baseline.
findings: Sandbox (CAPEv2) runs covering 37 malware families, represented as heterogeneous behavior graphs.
A voting ensemble reached 94.44% accuracy and MCC 0.863.
A multiclass model could tell apart 24 malware families.
papers.takeaway: Behavior graphs give defenders a richer signal than flat indicators; sandbox behavior can differ from what malware does in the wild.
papers.evidence: Preprint · sandbox dataset across 37 malware families

papers.title: Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime
papers.authors: Alexander Krentsel, Sylvia Ratnasamy, Ion Stoica
papers.summary: Letting an agent system improve itself while it runs cut model costs by 12%–53% versus Codex and Pi at the same completion rates, and by 45%–82% when lessons were transferred to new runs.
findings: Standalone runs: 12%–53% lower model cost than Codex and Pi with matching completion rates.
On held-out AppWorld and SREGym tasks, cost fell 35%–61%.
AppWorld task time dropped 13% and median SREGym diagnosis time dropped 35%.
papers.takeaway: Runtime self-improvement could make agents cheaper and faster without retraining; results are from a few agent benchmarks.
papers.evidence: Preprint · systems evaluation on agent benchmarks

papers.title: Perceived Trust and Transparency in AI-Altered vs. Human-Written LinkedIn Posts
papers.authors: Thomas Christian Joos, Azza Bouleimen, Anikó Hannák
papers.summary: Readers could not tell when an AI had polished someone's LinkedIn post: they spotted AI alteration only 49% of the time, and the alteration itself did not change how trustworthy or transparent posts seemed.
findings: Pre-registered within-subjects online experiment with 214 participants rating unlabeled human-written and AI-altered posts.
AI alteration had a near-zero, non-significant effect on trust and transparency; detection accuracy was 49%, and unsure readers assumed a human wrote it.
More detailed editing prompts raised trust and transparency but made edits easier to spot; posts where the AI added a new, invented idea were rated as more trustworthy.
papers.takeaway: AI-polished posts pass as human and can even gain credibility from invented content, which weakens trust cues online; the study covers one LinkedIn-style format.

papers.title: Whose Guardrail? User Identity Shapes the Effectiveness of Model Disclaimers in Mitigating LLM Political Persuasion
papers.authors: Jillian Fisher, Thomas Richardson, Daniel W. Fisher
papers.summary: Warning labels on a politically biased chatbot only partly protected people from being swayed: disclaimers naming the bias and explaining it reduced persuasion, but the effect varied by task and had faded a week later (1,586 participants).
findings: Pre-registered experiment with 1,586 participants who did two decision tasks with an LLM biased against their own politics, measured immediately and one week later.
Disclaimers that flagged political bias with an explanation cut persuasion; effects were inconsistent across tasks and did not persist to the follow-up.
Who the user was mattered more: Republicans were more persuaded and more trusting than Democrats, frequent AI users were more persuaded, and self-rated AI-savvy users less.
papers.takeaway: One-size disclaimers are a weak guardrail against AI persuasion; the abstract gives no effect sizes.

papers.title: Active Learning with Generative AI in Introductory Physics: A Multi-Institutional Study of the P-A.I.R. Framework
papers.authors: Bilas Paul, Shantanu Chakraborty, Shruti Shrestha
papers.summary: When physics students used AI in a set cycle (get a worked solution, then solve AI-made look-alike problems on their own), 90.9% said their conceptual understanding improved, and their confidence tracked how they used AI, not how often.
findings: Tested in 11 introductory physics sections at four U.S. institutions with a shared end-of-semester survey.
90.9% reported better conceptual understanding and 97.7% found the replicated practice problems helpful; mean confidence was 7.18 out of 10.
Confidence correlated with perceived understanding (r_s = 0.37) but not with frequency of AI use (r_s = 0.02); top concerns were AI accuracy (34.2%) and wanting guidance rather than answers (29.7%).
papers.takeaway: Structuring AI help around independent practice looks promising for physics courses, but the evidence is self-reported survey data with no control group or test scores.
papers.evidence: Multi-site survey · 11 course sections, 4 institutions · no control group

papers.title: Analysis of Local Open-Weight LLM Agents on Vulnerability-Reproduction Tasks
papers.authors: Jorge García-Carrasco, Javier Sanchis, Álvaro Navarro
papers.summary: Open-weight models running on a single consumer GPU can reproduce real software vulnerabilities: every configuration down to a 4B model solved most of the six easier CyberGym tasks, though the harder four needed the 27B model.
findings: Twelve local model configurations (three generations, two architectures, three quantization levels) tested on ten CyberGym tasks, three runs each.
Quantization never changed which tasks were solved in matched pairs, only how fast; the mixture-of-experts model hit the same scores in less wall-clock time.
Nearly every run, including failures, found the vulnerable function and the right hypothesis; success hinged on turning that hypothesis into a working crashing input.
papers.takeaway: Security teams can do private, local vulnerability reproduction with small models, but the test set is only ten tasks.
papers.evidence: Preprint · benchmark of 12 local model configs on 10 tasks

papers.title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
papers.authors: Xinrui Zhong, Zhiming Wang, Yongqi Liu
papers.summary: Coding agents can build LLM serving systems that beat standard software, but not reliably: the best run (Claude Sonnet 5.5) delivered 4.87x the value per GPU dollar of the vLLM reference, yet only 22 of 33 runs produced a system that passed verification.
findings: Benchmark across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, scored on latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost, with independent verification of each system.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 reached 2.97 "dollars per dollar" on Gemma E4B, 4.87x vLLM.
22 of 33 runs gave verified systems and 13 beat the strongest baseline; winning designs combined capacity gains with smart load selection.
papers.takeaway: Agents can now do real systems-optimization work, but a third of attempts failed verification, so independent checks remain essential.
papers.evidence: Preprint · benchmark of 11 agent models, 33 runs

papers.title: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
papers.authors: Amir Dehkordi, Alireza Kargarzadeh, Nariman Khaledian
papers.summary: Under a strict anti-look-ahead protocol, language models reading company news could not beat the market: the best fine-tuned signal fell to a daily information coefficient of 0.020 (t = 1.7) on a blinded 2026 test, and no pre-registered strategy survived trading costs.
findings: The fine-tuned model's signal held on two validation quarters (IC 0.055 and 0.065) before shrinking on the blinded January–July 2026 test.
Commercial models tracked the overnight move to the open (IC 0.074–0.077) but not returns after the open, suggesting news is priced in before a trader can act.
Masking names did not hide companies: commercial models identified masked firms in 62%–74% of cases versus a 28% baseline.
papers.takeaway: Many reported LLM news-trading gains may reflect look-ahead and memorization; this test covers S&P 500 stocks over a short seven-month window.
papers.evidence: Pre-registered backtest · S&P 500 news, blinded Jan–Jul 2026 test

papers.title: How market volatility responds to a preceding price trend: a lag-resolved measurement in cryptocurrencies and equities
papers.authors: Gulsah Bicki, Taylan Akdogan
papers.summary: In Bitcoin and Ether, price trends predict later volatility with a leverage-effect-like asymmetry that peaks at a 20-minute lag and halves within about 1.5 hours; large U.S. stocks showed no detectable one-way (time-asymmetric) component at 20 minutes.
findings: One-minute data from 2020–2026 for three large cryptocurrencies on one exchange, three large U.S. stocks and the S&P 500 ETF.
For Bitcoin and Ether, the time-asymmetric part of the response was 0.4–0.9 of the symmetric part at the first lag, consistent with a purely one-sided response at 20 minutes.
Checks on simulated and shuffled data returned zero within expected error and recovered a planted response time scale.
papers.takeaway: Suggests crypto volatility reacts to trends in a directional way that equities do not show at this scale; the sample is small (a few assets, one exchange) and a small opposite-sign effect is unresolved.

papers.title: Signals, Evidence, and Context: User Scrutiny in Real-World LLM Conversations
papers.authors: Ahana Biswas, Yu-Ru Lin
papers.summary: In nearly half a million real chatbot exchanges, cues like source attribution and hedging rarely tipped users toward fact-checking rather than pushing back; only expressed uncertainty showed a small pooled link with checking.
findings: Analyzed 489,283 assistant reply–user follow-up pairs drawn from the ShareChat and WildChat logs.
Vague attribution language ("studies show") appeared in 31.9% of eligible replies, while actual URLs appeared in just 1.33%.

Effects depended on context: uncertainty favored checking in technical help, while refusals and visible reasoning favored challenging in information-seeking; apparent carry-over of scrutiny across turns shrank a lot after accounting for conversation-level differences.
papers.takeaway: Suggests the trust cues chatbots display do not reliably steer people toward verifying answers; the data are observational logs, so the links are associations, not causal effects.
papers.evidence: Preprint · observational log analysis · 489,283 conversation pairs

papers.title: Automated Feedback to Peer Tutors Increases Their Talk Moves and Learner Reasoning but Not the Balance of Talk
papers.authors: Dorottya Demszky, Yann Hicke, Joy Yun
papers.summary: Giving volunteer math tutors automated feedback on how they talk raised their use of good teaching moves and students' reasoning by 8–15%, but tutors still did about 91.5% of the talking.
findings: Randomized trial in two four-week SAT math bootcamps on Schoolhouse.world: 1,030 volunteer tutors, 7,443 learners, 6,508 recorded sessions.
Tutor feedback increased eliciting learner ideas, building on learner contributions, and learner reasoning by 8–15%; the pattern replicated in both bootcamps.

Tutor share of talk time averaged 91.5% in the control group and did not change in any condition; adding participation feedback for learners gave no further change. Interviews (17 tutors, 13 learners) pointed to unresponsive learners and learners' preference for listening.
papers.takeaway: Shows low-cost automated discourse feedback can improve peer tutoring at scale, but nudging tutors alone does not get quiet learners to talk more.

papers.title: KG-AST for Cheaper CI/CD: Budgeted Test Selection and AI Bug Review
papers.authors: Henry Yeung
papers.summary: Focusing heavy testing on the 20% of commits a model flags as riskiest caught 49–64% of bug-introducing commits across 155 projects, beating the 'biggest change first' rule in every language.
findings: Across 155 open-source projects in 11 languages, the model beat the biggest-change baseline (40–55% coverage) by 3.8 to 13.2 points; random picking catches about 20%.
In 20 Java projects at a 20% budget it covered 64.6% vs 49.5% (+15.1 points), winning in 19 of 20 projects.

An AI reviewer that saw only the diff pinpointed 26% of later-fixed defects (32% with code-graph context); a call-graph test selector ran about 8% of tests and hit a fix-related test in 85% of 67 fix commits.
papers.takeaway: Offers a practical way to cut CI costs while still catching most risky changes; single-author preprint, and one component (Poincaré embeddings) added nothing.
papers.evidence: Preprint · retrospective evaluation · 155 open-source projects, 11 languages

papers.title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
papers.authors: Xiaobo Chen, Genliang Zhu, Ziyuan Wang
papers.summary: Cryptographically signing the requirements one AI agent hands to another cut unsafe actions under attack from 69.4% to 9.0%, but a single adversarial line slipped in before signing pushed violations as high as 75%.
findings: Preregistered study on scorable synthetic tasks; with Qwen3-8B (1,440 runs, five threat types) signed manifests cut unsafe commits from 69.4% to 9.0% without losing correct commits.
A deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions with 7% false alarms, versus 59.0% and 50% for an LLM-based checker.
Injecting one adversarial line before signing raised violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna).
papers.takeaway: Signing protects requirements in transit but not what goes into them, so multi-agent pipelines still need checks on how requirements are written; results come from synthetic tasks.

papers.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
papers.authors: Xiangkai Zeng, Zheng Liu, Zihao Lin
papers.summary: When coding agents must keep building on their own earlier code over 5–15 dependent steps, the best of nine frontier models solves only 18.5% of tasks.
findings: Benchmark of 69 software tasks, each a chain of 5–15 dependent steps, across nine programming languages.
The strongest of nine frontier models reached an 18.5% solve rate.
38 of the 69 tasks were not solved by any model.
papers.takeaway: Suggests single-issue benchmarks overstate how well agents handle sustained development; the benchmark is fairly small (69 tasks).
papers.evidence: Preprint · benchmark of 9 frontier models · 69 tasks

papers.title: EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments
papers.authors: Mingxuan Li, Huanzhi Mao, Qiuyang Mang
papers.summary: Automatically reshaping the workspace and data an agent works in, without changing the model, cut Claude Haiku 4.5's cost on AutomationBench by 72.7% while raising its pass rate by 14.34%.
findings: The environment optimized for Haiku 4.5 transferred to Opus 5, cutting cost by 68.1% with a 1.34% pass-rate gain.
Stacked on an already optimized Meta-Harness setup, it cut cost a further 83.4% and added 11.17% accuracy.
Across five benchmarks it lowered cost while improving or holding pass rate, without needing graders or reference answers.
papers.takeaway: Points to the agent's environment as a third tuning lever next to model weights and harness code; gains are measured on benchmarks, not live deployments.

papers.title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
papers.authors: E. Kelly Buchanan, Crystal Zhou, Scott W. Linderman
papers.summary: An audit found problems in about 30% of Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks; fixing them raised agent accuracy by over 10 percentage points and moved leaderboard positions by up to three ranks.
findings: Repairs are released as Terminal-Bench 2.1; overall rankings stayed highly correlated with the old version (Spearman ρ = 0.958).
Longer time limits closed a 20-point harness gap for GPT 5.4 and shrank a 30-point gap for GPT 5.4 mini to 5 points.
The authors argue benchmarks need ongoing maintenance like software.
papers.takeaway: A reminder that headline agent scores partly reflect benchmark bugs and time limits; broad rankings held up, but close comparisons may not.

papers.title: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems
papers.authors: Yao Huang, Yichi Zhang, Yifan Wang
papers.summary: A loss-of-control risk score built from 29 behavioral tests tracked how often 13 frontier models failed in contained long-horizon scenarios (r = 0.84), and risk was not explained by capability alone.
findings: Splits risk into misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability and monitoring evasion, measured via 13 aspects and 29 evaluation tasks.
Across 13 frontier models the combined score correlated with scenario failure rates at Pearson r = 0.84.
Targeted fine-tuning and monitoring for diagnosed weaknesses lowered failure rates while largely keeping general performance (no figures given).
papers.takeaway: Offers a measurable way to compare control risk across models; it is validated on contained test scenarios with 13 models, not real-world incidents.
papers.evidence: Preprint · evaluation study · 13 frontier models, 29 tasks

papers.title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance
papers.authors: Yupeng Cao, Xueqing Peng, Lingfei Qian
papers.summary: Asked to gather data, build and backtest a client's hidden trading strategy, AI agents passed zero of 150 sessions; even runs the simulated client approved failed at least one program check.
findings: Four coding agents and one tool-less model were tested in 150 sessions; acceptance required client satisfaction and passing all 15 veto checks.
Agents surfaced only 54–64% of the strategy details they were not explicitly told.
Human experts attributed 88.33% of failures to the agents; with the benchmark's feedback, an agent with persistent memory eventually learned all ten tasks.
papers.takeaway: Warns that AI agents can produce finance analyses a client is happy with that are still wrong; the users are simulated and the task set is small (ten tasks).

papers.title: Return Decomposition of Hybrid Strategies in the Brazilian Market: Evidence of Genuine Alpha and Factor Exposure
papers.authors: Francisco Robson do Nascimento de Freitas, Felipe Macedo Zumba, Lucio Marassi
papers.summary: A Brazilian stock strategy mixing value/quality screens with a moving-average trend rule earned about 1% a month of risk-adjusted excess return (alpha) over 2000–2025, after controlling for standard factors.
findings: 300 monthly observations on B3, Jan 2000–Dec 2025; three-factor alpha 1.11%/month (p = 0.005), four-factor alpha 0.98%/month (p = 0.009).
Exposure to small caps was strong (SMB beta 0.38) while value and momentum loadings were not significant; market beta about 0.58.
Sharpe ratio was 0.443 vs 0.039 for the Ibovespa, but that difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.154).
papers.takeaway: Suggests simple combined rules may still earn excess returns in an emerging market, but it is a single backtest without stated trading costs, and the Sharpe gain is not significant.

papers.title: Neural Realized Measures: Forecast-Supervised Intraday Aggregation for Volatility Forecasting
papers.authors: Brian Sing Fan Chan, Jennifer So Kuen Chan
papers.summary: Letting a neural network learn how to weight intraday returns improved crypto volatility forecasts in all 54 out-of-sample comparisons, by about 7–9% on average.
findings: Tested on six cryptocurrencies with five-minute data under three standard forecasting models.
Mean QLIKE loss improvements were 7.23% (SF), 8.15% (HAR) and 9.22% (MIDAS).
In Heston-model simulations it also lowered forecast error for same-day and next-day variance in every tested setting.
papers.takeaway: A drop-in upgrade for volatility forecasting inputs; evidence is limited to six crypto assets, so it is untested on equities.
